stories.text: Florence Boot, born in St Helier, Jersey, in 1863, married Jesse Boot in 1886 and helped him run the firm. She brought books and stationery into the Goose Gate shop and started Boots Book-Lovers' Library and cafés in the stores. She founded the university's first hall for women, named Florence Boot Hall after her.
Louisa May Long (1892–1981), who nursed with the 94 Nottingham VAD at Radcliffe on Trent in the First World War, was Matron of Florence Boot Hall from 1928 to 1946.

stories.text: On the night of 8–9 May 1941 the Luftwaffe bombed Nottingham. Firefighters saved St Mary's Church after an incendiary burned through its roof; three Boots factories, in Poplar Street, Island Street and Station Street, were on fire; University College and the Shakespeare Street chapel were hit. The worst loss was at the Co-op bakery on Meadow Lane, where 49 people died. In all, 159 people were killed that night.

Vera Anderson, a Boots nurse, was on duty when bombs wrecked the Boots Printing Works here on 8 May 1941. She gave first aid to a dying night watchman through burning debris, then treated casualties at the control centre, and was awarded the George Medal.

72531.sum: Trent House is the European headquarters of the finance company Capital One. It is on Station Street to the south of the centre of the English city of Nottingham, opposite Nottingham railway station and adjacent to Loxley House, the administrative headquarters of Nottingham City Council. The building dates from 1951, when it was built as a print works for the pharmaceutical company Boots, whose various premises occupied most of the surrounding area at that time.

stories.text: After a riot in Fleet Street, Richard II summoned the mayor, sheriffs and aldermen of London to appear before him and his council at Nottingham Castle on 25 June 1392. The mayor and sheriffs were removed from their offices and imprisoned, and a royal warden was put in charge of the City: London lost its self-government until it had paid the king to win it back.

While Richard I was away, the castle was held by supporters of his brother, Prince John, among them the Sheriff of Nottingham. In March 1194 King Richard came and besieged it, building siege machines like those he had used on crusade.

King John took hostages in numbers no king had before. In 1212, when the Welsh rose against him, he came to Nottingham with his army and, the chronicler Roger of Wendover says, before he either ate or drank had twenty-eight youths hanged, whom he had received from the Welsh as hostages the year before.[^wendover] The Magna Carta Project puts them at some thirty, and calls it notorious.[^mcp]

stories.text: When the House of Lords threw out the Second Reform Bill on 8 October 1831, rioting broke out in Nottingham and a crowd burned the castle, which belonged to the Duke of Newcastle, an opponent of reform. Three men were hanged; the Duke refused to restore the castle, and its burnt shell stood on the rock for years.

After Henry IV's queen, Joan of Navarre, lived here until 1437, the castle was little kept up, until the Wars of the Roses made it a stronghold again.[^s1] Edward IV proclaimed himself king in Nottingham, and in 1476 ordered a new tower and royal apartments, which John Leland, writing in 1540, thought the finest part of the castle.[^s1] On 20 August 1485 Richard III rode from Nottingham to Leicester, two days before he was killed at Bosworth.[^s2]

In 1643 Colonel John Hutchinson took command of Nottingham Castle, and Parliament later made him governor of both town and castle. It was a hard post: the town had no walls, the garrison was small and short of supplies, and the committee that ran the town quarrelled. Hutchinson held on all the same, and protected the radical separatists among his soldiers as far as he could.

The burnt mansion stood a ruin until Thomas Chambers Hine restored it in 1875. The Prince of Wales opened it in 1878 as Nottingham Castle Museum, the first municipal art gallery in the United Kingdom outside London. The castle closed in 2018 for a redevelopment that cost £30 million, and reopened on 21 June 2021 under the charity Nottingham Castle Trust. In November 2022 the trust said it was appointing liquidators, and the site went back to the council.

The first castle on the rock was a wooden motte-and-bailey, begun in 1068 on William the Conqueror's orders, and rebuilt in stone under Henry II. For centuries it was a royal fortress and an occasional royal residence. After the Civil War it was razed in 1651, and in the 1670s the 1st Duke of Newcastle began a mansion on the rock. Rioters burnt the mansion in 1831; it reopened as a museum in 1878.

The Royalists of Newark raided again and again. Sir Charles Lucas broke into the town in January 1644 and tried to set it on fire, and in April 1645 a party from Newark took the fort at Trent Bridge. Each time Hutchinson won back what was lost, and each demand that he surrender the castle he answered with fresh defiance.

A regiment raised in 1741 became, at the request of the people of Nottinghamshire, the 45th (1st Nottinghamshire) Regiment of Foot in 1779.[^s1] Against Napoleon it fought through the Peninsular War from 1808 to 1814, and at Talavera in 1809 won the nickname "Old Stubborns".[^s1] Renamed the Sherwood Foresters in 1866, it was joined with the Derbyshire regiment on 1 July 1881 as the Sherwood Foresters (Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire Regiment), whose museum is in the castle.[^s1]

Henry VIII sent new tapestries ahead of his visit in August 1511, but a survey of 1525 found the castle in "dekay and ruyne", part of the Great Hall's roof fallen in. It was garrisoned again in 1536, against the Pilgrimage of Grace, and in 1562 it was to host a meeting of Elizabeth I and Mary, Queen of Scots, which never took place. By 1600 it was no longer a royal home.

In 1995 the Design Museum in London put on True Brit, a show marking 25 years of the fashion business of Paul Smith, who was born in Beeston. It went on to Glasgow and then to his home city, where it was shown in Nottingham Castle.
Kate Watson Wallis (1852–1918), a suffragist, lived in the Residence at the Castle with her husband, the Castle Art Gallery's first curator.

74050.sum: Nottingham Castle is a Stuart Restoration-era ducal mansion in Nottingham, England, built on the site of a Norman castle built starting in 1068, and added to extensively through the medieval period, when it was an important royal fortress and occasional royal residence. In decline by the 16th century, the original castle, except for its walls and gates, was demolished after the English Civil War in 1651.

74412.sum: The Church of St Mary the Virgin is the oldest parish church in Nottingham, England. The church is Grade I listed by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport as a building of outstanding architectural or historic interest. It is one of only five Grade I listed buildings in the City of Nottingham.

stories.text: John Boot opened a herbalist's shop on Goose Gate in 1849, and his son Jesse was born in the area, into poverty, the next year.[^boots] After John died in 1860 his widow Mary kept the shop going as M & J Boot.[^boots] Jesse became a partner at 21, and in 1883 he built a larger store on the same site, the first of the Boots shops; Nottingham Civic Society put up a plaque here in 2015.[^boots]

stories.text: The building began in 1839 as a grand Wesleyan chapel on Broad Street. Broadway opened here in 1990, and one of its screens is the only cinema screen designed by Sir Paul Smith.

Hockley has a taste for small cinema. Broadway was the first cinema in the UK to show Quentin Tarantino's Pulp Fiction, and from 2002 to 2011 the district also had The Screen Room, then the smallest commercial cinema in the world.

74666.sum: Broadway Cinema is an independent cinema and registered charity in Nottingham, England, located in the Hockley area of the city's Creative Quarter. With a mission to inspire creativity and a lifelong love of film, Broadway is one of the UK's leading independent cinemas, attracting circa 200,000 visitors annually to its four-screen cinema, café bar, and creative workspace.

stories.text: Boots' central store was built on the corner of Pelham Street and High Street to designs by Albert Nelson Bromley: 1902–05 by Historic England's dates, 1903–04 in Wikipedia's list of his works.[^s1] Its shopfront, with curving Art Nouveau panels, has hardly changed and is a rare survivor of its kind.[^he] Historic England suggests it may be the first Art Nouveau shopfront in the country, and that Harrods inspired it.[^hc][^report] Boots left in 1972; Zara trades here now.[^report]

The building was converted in 1953 to a synagogue and is now a university hall. Whilst in use as a synagogue, in 1972 the building was listed as a Grade II building.

Built in 1877–81 for University College Nottingham, with the town's library and a natural history museum, and damaged by bombs in the Second World War. D. H. Lawrence studied here to become a teacher; it is now Nottingham Trent University's Arkwright Building.

76264.sum: The Arkwright Building is a Grade II* listed university building on Shakespeare Street in Nottingham, England. It forms part of the Nottingham Trent University City Campus and is one of the university's principal historic buildings. Built between 1877 and 1881, the building was originally home to University College Nottingham, the city library and a natural history museum.

stories.text: Iron-working at Stanton grew into a huge concern from the 1780s. By the mid-19th century the works made 20,000 tons of iron castings a year, and 2.5 million by 1905. From 1985 the French Saint-Gobain group ran it, and the last casting, in 2007, was an emotional day. The pin is approximate.

114885.sum: Saint-Gobain PAM UK: Head Office is an office building on Low's Lane.

stories.text: James Shipstone founded the Star Brewery in New Basford in 1852. The red-brick building of 1900 had a red illuminated star on its tower that could be seen for miles. Greenall's of Warrington bought the firm in 1978 and stopped brewing in early 1991; the building now belongs to an auction house.

John Robinson founded the Home Brewery in 1875; its beer mats carried a Robin Hood badge. The family sold it in 1986, and its closure cost some 400 jobs. Its building of 1936 is now Sir John Robinson House, and listed Grade II.

273134.sum: Home Ales Brewery Office, on Sir John Robinson Way. Today it houses Home Brewery Building, an office. It is Grade II listed and was designed by T Cecil Howitt.

stories.text: Ibuprofen was first made at Boots in Nottingham in December 1961, by Stewart Adams's team. Their later laboratory, on Pennyfoot Street, is now BioCity, and in 2013 a Royal Society of Chemistry blue plaque marked the discovery. Adams and the chemist John Nicholson filed the patent in 1961; the drug was first sold in Britain in 1969, as Brufen, and in 1983 it became the first such painkiller apart from aspirin sold over the counter in the UK.[^ibu]

In 1920 Boots bought a site on Oakfields Road for pharmacological and bacteriological research, which was done here until new laboratories were built in 1956; the site was sold in 1964.[^gateway] With its city-centre labs damaged in the war, Boots put research into converted houses in West Bridgford.[^boots] From 1953 to 1959 Stewart Adams worked in one of the front rooms of a house here, a rather primitive laboratory,[^odnb] while his technician used the larder as an office.[^boots] On Rutland Road, in August 1958, his team began to study the phenoxy acids, the line of work that led to ibuprofen.[^wiki] The day nursery on the corner of Oakfields Road and Rutland Road was also part of Boots.[^lb]
